title: Контроль на каждом шагу  (Control at Every Step)

segments.t: At Arcobaleno, Viktor snaps at Elena for watching his every move in the kitchen, while back at Claude Monet German catches sous-chef Lyova helping Denis and orders him onto potato duty. Listen in Russian first.
Пойди в салон красоты, что-нибудь сделай.
С этого момента отправляйтесь на заготовки.
Let's look closely at each Russian line in this scene.
'Did you not forget the salt?' Putting the short word for 'not' right in front of the action word is all Russian needs to make a sentence negative, with no extra helper words like 'do' or 'did'.
'I did not forget anything at all.' Chef Barinov centers this short reply on 'to forget', letting a few direct words carry the whole meaning.
'Why are you controlling everything in here?' In spoken Russian, the words stay in their normal statement order and Chef Barinov's rising voice at the end turns the line into a question.
'You have been following me around all day.' Here Chef Barinov anchors the thought on 'are walking' and finishes on 'day', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
'Do you have nothing else to do?' Chef Viktor addresses the listener with the informal singular pronoun, showing a close or familiar relationship.
Пойди в салон красоты, что-нибудь сделай.
'Go to a beauty salon, do something for yourself.' Chef Barinov pairs 'to go' with 'make' directly, since spoken Russian skips English filler words like 'the', 'a', and 'is'.
'Sorry, I got carried away...' Spoken Russian keeps this brief and expressive, built right around 'sorry' without extra helper words.
'Would you care for a massage as well?' In spoken Russian, the words stay in their normal statement order and German's rising voice at the end turns the line into a question.
С этого момента отправляйтесь на заготовки.
'From this moment on, report to vegetable prep.' In everyday Russian, 'moment' flows straight into 'preparation' without extra linking words.
'Go peel potatoes.' German pairs 'to peel, clean, scrape' with 'potatoes' directly, since spoken Russian skips English filler words like 'the', 'a', and 'is'.
'Alright, Viktor Petrovich.' Spoken Russian keeps this brief and expressive, built right around 'good, well, all right' without extra helper words.
'Get to work.' German centers this short reply on 'work', letting a few direct words carry the whole meaning. With all the phrases clear, listen to the full Russian dialogue again.
Пойди в салон красоты, что-нибудь сделай.
С этого момента отправляйтесь на заготовки.
That covers Viktor snapping at Elena for hovering over him and advising her to visit a beauty salon. Notice how Russian reflexive verbs express finding something to do. Until next time!
